annotation_description: With a hand containing no 1-drop creatures and a curve starting at 2 mana (Deep-Cavern Bat), choosing to play first means drawing one fewer card. The hand has Kaito (4 mana) and two Deep-Cavern Bats but limited early pressure and no turn-1 play. On the draw, the extra card could help find additional lands or action. However, going first does allow Turn 2 Deep-Cavern Bat to strip a card before the opponent develops, which is a legitimate tempo play. This is close but the hand's mana base (Island, Swamp, Multiversal Passage, Soulstone Sanctuary) is a bit awkward and an extra draw could help smooth things out.

Playing Multiversal Passage on turn 1 when there are no turn-1 plays wastes the flexibility of this dual-purpose land. With Island, Swamp, and Soulstone Sanctuary also in hand, playing a basic land first preserves Multiversal Passage's ability to fill whatever color gap emerges later. The hand wants B on turn 2 for Deep-Cavern Bat and UB by turn 4 for Kaito — playing Swamp turn 1 achieves the same curve while keeping Multiversal Passage flexible.

Playing Willowrush Verge instead of Breeding Pool on turn 1 is suboptimal. Willowrush Verge can only tap for {U} on turn 1 (it needs a Forest or Island to tap for {G}). If Breeding Pool were played (paying 2 life to enter untapped), it would be both a Forest and an Island, enabling Willowrush Verge to tap for {G} on turn 2. More importantly, playing Breeding Pool turn 1 allows casting Llanowar Elves or Gene Pollinator immediately this turn, developing the board a full turn earlier. With Willowrush Verge, the player can only produce {U} this turn and cannot cast their {G} one-drops.

Playing Swamp instead of Island means the player cannot cast Deep-Cavern Bat on turn 2 (which costs {1}{B} and could be cast with Multiversal Passage choosing Swamp + Island for the {1}). Wait - Multiversal Passage was already chosen as a basic land type when it entered. Let me reconsider. The Multiversal Passage chose a basic land type on entry. We don't know what type was chosen. If it was chosen as Swamp, then playing Island would give access to both {B} and {U}, enabling Deep-Cavern Bat (1B) with either land providing the generic, AND keeping Floodpits Drowner (1U) as an option. If Multiversal Passage was chosen as Island, then playing Swamp enables Deep-Cavern Bat but not Floodpits Drowner. Playing Island would mean two Islands and no black mana. So the choice depends on what Multiversal Passage was set to. Given MiMo paid 2 life (went from 20 to 18) to have it enter untapped, and the hand has Deep-Cavern Bat and Kaito requiring black, it was likely chosen as Swamp. With Multiversal Passage as Swamp, playing Island would give {B} + {U} enabling both Deep-Cavern Bat AND holding up Floodpits Drowner as options. Playing Swamp gives {B}{B} which only enables Deep-Cavern Bat but not Floodpits Drowner. Island would have been more flexible, keeping open the option to flash in Floodpits Drowner if the opponent plays a threatening creature.

With 3 lands available (Multiversal Passage, Swamp, and the Island about to be played), MiMo could cast Deep-Cavern Bat (1B) this turn to look at the opponent's hand and potentially exile a key card. Playing Island instead of Soulstone Sanctuary is fine, but the real issue is not following up by casting Deep-Cavern Bat. However, looking at the choices more carefully, the decision is specifically about which card to play from the four options. Deep-Cavern Bat costs {1}{B} and MiMo has Swamp + Multiversal Passage (chosen as a basic land type - we don't know which type). If Multiversal Passage was chosen as Island or Swamp, then with Swamp + Multiversal Passage they might have the mana. But they also have Floodpits Drowner on the battlefield (untapped 2/1 with vigilance). Playing Island and then casting Deep-Cavern Bat with Swamp + Island/Passage would work if they have {1}{B}. Actually, the choices show Island AND Deep-Cavern Bat as separate options - they could potentially play Island AND then cast Deep-Cavern Bat. But since this is the chosen action (Island over Deep-Cavern Bat), and the game shows the turn then passes to Qwen3 Timmy, it seems MiMo only played the Island and didn't cast Deep-Cavern Bat. Deep-Cavern Bat on turn 3 is a strong tempo play - it provides hand information, can exile a threat, and has evasion + lifelink. Missing this deployment is a real missed opportunity.

Playing Soulstone Sanctuary instead of Deep-Cavern Bat is suboptimal. With 2 mana available (Multiversal Passage + Swamp, or Island + Swamp), MiMo could cast Deep-Cavern Bat to see the opponent's hand, potentially exile a key card like Nature's Rhythm or Craterhoof Behemoth, gain incremental lifelink damage, and still have the land drop available next turn. Deep-Cavern Bat is a tempo play that provides critical information and disruption while also adding a flying attacker alongside Floodpits Drowner. Playing Soulstone Sanctuary (a colorless land that enters untapped) doesn't enable anything meaningful this turn that couldn't wait - the 4-mana activation is expensive and the extra mana isn't needed immediately. The bat gives information, disruption, evasive pressure, and lifelink.

Hard-casting Kaito precombat instead of using his Ninjutsu ability. Deep-Cavern Bat has flying and can't be blocked by Llanowar Elves, making it a perfect Ninjutsu enabler. Using Ninjutsu would cost only 3 mana instead of 4, return Deep-Cavern Bat to hand for a future ETB trigger (hand disruption), and still get Kaito attacking as a 3/4.

MiMo Gramps had exactly enough mana (Island + Island + Swamp + Soulstone Sanctuary = {2}{U}{U}) to flash in Enduring Curiosity before combat damage. With Floodpits Drowner and Deep-Cavern Bat both dealing combat damage to the opponent, Enduring Curiosity would have triggered twice, drawing 2 cards. The opponent's board was just a Llanowar Elves with no untapped blue mana for counterplay.

MiMo Gramps spent 4 mana to animate Soulstone Sanctuary into a 3/3 vigilance creature instead of casting Enduring Curiosity (4/3 flash with massive card draw potential). With Floodpits Drowner and Deep-Cavern Bat already on board, Enduring Curiosity would draw cards whenever any creature deals combat damage, providing significant card advantage. The opponent is at 11 life with almost no board, making the card advantage engine extremely powerful. Enduring Curiosity is also resilient to removal (returns as enchantment when it dies).

Discarding Spider-Sense, the only counterspell/interaction piece in hand, against a UB control/tempo deck that likely has removal spells and threats like Kaito. With 5 mana creatures already in hand (2 Spider Manifestation, 2 Gene Pollinator, 1 Llanowar Elves) plus one on board, discarding a redundant mana dork would preserve the ability to interact with the opponent's key spells.

MiMo Gramps used Shoot the Sheriff to kill Llanowar Elves during combat instead of using Kaito's Ninjutsu ability to put Kaito onto the battlefield as an unblocked attacker. With Floodpits Drowner attacking unblocked, Ninjutsu for {1}{U}{B} would deploy a 3/4 hexproof threat that generates emblems and card advantage. The available mana (Island, Swamp, Multiversal Passage as Island, Soulstone Sanctuary) likely couldn't support both plays, making this a choice between killing a 1/1 mana dork and deploying a game-winning planeswalker.

MiMo Gramps used Shoot the Sheriff to destroy the opponent's Llanowar Elves instead of one of their own creatures that was a valid target. Shoot the Sheriff says 'Destroy target non-outlaw creature' — it can target any non-outlaw creature on either side. However, looking at the context more carefully: MiMo Gramps is the one casting Shoot the Sheriff, so they're choosing what to kill. Llanowar Elves is the opponent's mana dork, while Floodpits Drowner and Deep-Cavern Bat are MiMo's own creatures. Killing the opponent's Llanowar Elves removes their mana acceleration when they're already at 11 life with only 2 lands. However, this is being cast during MiMo's own combat phase, which means MiMo spent mana on removal during their own attack step rather than before or after combat. More importantly, the Deep-Cavern Bat is tapped (likely attacked or just entered), and Floodpits Drowner could have attacked. The real question is whether killing Llanowar Elves was the right target — and it actually seems reasonable since it denies the opponent mana. But casting a removal spell during your own combat phase is unusual timing. Actually, re-reading: the opponent has Spider-Sense in graveyard, so no counterspell threat. Killing Llanowar Elves to deny mana when the opponent is at 11 life and only has 2 lands is actually a reasonable play to keep them constrained. This seems fine.

Paid 2 life for Breeding Pool to enter untapped at 8 life when facing 3 damage per turn from opponent's creatures. The extra untapped mana enables casting an additional 1-drop alongside a 2-drop, but at 8 life (going to 6), every life point is critical. With 2 lands already available, they could still cast their key 2-mana plays (Badgermole Cub or Spider Manifestation) without the life payment.

With the opponent having no untapped creatures to block and no mana available for instant-speed interaction, attacking with only Breeding Pool instead of all available creatures leaves free damage on the table. Spider Manifestation could attack for 2 additional damage risk-free.

MiMo Gramps missed lethal. Opponent is at 5 life with only Spider Manifestation (2/2 reach) as a blocker and all lands tapped. By using Kaito's +1 (making him a 4/5 Ninja with the emblem), then casting Requiting Hex (B) to destroy Spider Manifestation (mana value 2), then attacking with Kaito (4/5) and Deep-Cavern Bat (1/1 flying) for exactly 5 damage = lethal. Instead, they played a tapped land and skipped their attack entirely.

MiMo Gramps missed lethal. Opponent is at 5 life with only Spider Manifestation (2/2 reach, MV 2) as a blocker. Requiting Hex destroys creatures with MV 2 or less, clearing the blocker. Then activating Soulstone Sanctuary (4 mana) to make it a 3/3 and attacking with Kaito (3/4) + Deep-Cavern Bat (1/1) + Soulstone creature (3/3) = 7 damage, lethal against 5 life.

Attacking with Deep-Cavern Bat (which is exiling Craterhoof Behemoth) alongside Kaito risks the opponent blocking and killing the bat to get Craterhoof back, all for just 1 extra damage when the opponent is at 5 life and this doesn't represent lethal. While the opponent at 5 life with minimal board may struggle to cast Craterhoof soon, unnecessarily risking the return of an 8-mana game-ending threat for marginal damage is suboptimal.

Discarded Craterhoof Behemoth, which is their only win condition. At 1 life the game is desperate, but Craterhoof is the only card that can convert a board of small creatures into a lethal attack. With mana creatures in hand and on board, reaching 8 mana was achievable within 1-2 turns. Without Craterhoof, there is essentially no path to winning.
